title: Charge 1% VAT on everything now zero-rated
headline: Charge 1% VAT on everything now zero-rated: IFS, £4.2bn.
description: Most food, children’s clothes, books, domestic passenger transport, new homes and prescriptions carry VAT at 0%. The IFS Green Budget scores a 1% rate on all of it at £4.2 billion in 2029-30, an alternative to the 20% toggles on this tab, which take one category at a time. Static and held flat in cash. A new positive rate on zero-rated goods is a VAT increase for the people who buy them, so the game treats it as breaking the tax lock.

baselinePolicy.text: Zero-rated goods and services carry VAT at 0% with input tax recoverable; the IFS puts the forgone revenue on food alone at £30.6 billion in 2029-30 and on new homes at £19.0 billion.

source.quote: Most food, for example, is zero-rated (representing an estimated £30.6 billion of forgone annual revenue in 2029–30)

alreadyIncludes: The zero rates as they stand, and the temporary zero rate on domestic electricity to March 2027.

terms.label: The IFS Green Budget’s yield from charging 1% VAT on all zero-rated products

source.quote: Charge 1% VAT on all zero-rated products £4.2 billion

rawSource.note: The IFS’s Table 9.3 figure for 2029-30, held flat in cash from the start year. Static.

caveats: Static, from the IFS’s ready-reckoner table; a small rate changes behaviour little, but the compliance cost of a new rate on food, books and children’s clothes is real.
Overlaps every zero-rate toggle on this tab: charging 20% on food and 1% on all zero-rated goods counts the same food twice. The cards warn each other.
A new rate on goods that carry none today is a VAT increase; the game treats it as breaking the manifesto lock.

considerations.text: The IFS’s £4.2 billion is a static figure from its table of options; at 1% the behavioural response is small, but retailers and HMRC would carry a new rate across the whole zero-rated base.

sources.quote: Charge 1% VAT on all zero-rated products £4.2 billion

considerations.text: Everyone who buys food, children’s clothes, books or a new home pays a little; the zero rates are worth most in cash to richer households but most as a share of spending to poorer ones.

sources.quote: By international standards, the UK VAT makes plentiful use of zero-rating

considerations.text: The manifesto promises not to increase VAT. A new 1% rate on goods that carry none today is an increase for the people who buy them, so the game treats this switch as breaking the tax lock.

sources.quote: we will not increase National Insurance, the basic, higher, or additional rates of Income Tax, or VAT
